source.title: Understanding Instance-Level Label Noise: Disparate Impacts and Treatments

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendix; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes memorization of noisy labels and its effects on generalization, but does not test any listed version about natural-label generalization, architecture, optimizers, batch size, regularization, model size, sharpness, or removing memorized examples.
record.gate_note: The paper's theory and CIFAR-10 illustration concern instance-level label noise and treatments for noisy labels. The natural-label and random-label generalization results it mentions are cited from prior work, not tested here.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes generalization under noisy-label memorization, conditional on a stipulated form of memorization. Its own results do not test any listed version: it reports neither the paired random-label/natural-label performance required by V1 nor the comparisons required by V2–V8. References to memorization benefiting generalization are prior-work claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, the authors derive frequency-dependent harms of noisy-label memorization and conditional treatment outcomes: frequent instances can incur larger generalization costs but are easier to correct, while rare instances retain non-negligible costs and substantial correction-failure probabilities. They recommend considering different treatments across frequency regimes.
record.recipe_differences: The paper provides theoretical analyses of instance-dependent noisy-label memorization and treatments, plus a CIFAR-10 illustration; it does not reproduce the natural-label/random-label experiments or other methods named in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Instance frequency and empirical noisy-label distribution affect the analyzed outcomes; the paper's peer-loss analysis also assumes class-dependent noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the stipulated memorization model, corrupted-label fractions and instance-frequency weights determine individual excessive generalization error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorizing noisy labels incurs a frequency-dependent generalization cost in the paper's theoretical framework.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet-34's normalized loss distributions overlap for clean and corrupted CIFAR-10 examples under both synthesized noise settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss distributions do not cleanly separate clean and corrupted training examples in the reported CIFAR-10 illustration.

fits_no_version.finding: Theoretical benefits and failures of loss correction, label smoothing, and peer loss depend on instance frequency and empirical label patterns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noisy-label treatments can help frequent instances while having substantial failure probabilities for rare instances; label smoothing and loss correction differ according to empirical label majorities.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 139, 2021
record.problems: Most version-relevant claim elements are not tested. The theoretical results rely on simplifying assumptions, including memorization of specified label distributions; the empirical CIFAR-10 result is described without numerical measures in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results on the listed versions were found. Cited prior-work findings were excluded because they are not results of this study.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels together with above-chance natural-label held-out accuracy and chance random-label held-out accuracy using the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Held-out error with versus without dropout across the specified regimes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness rankings of generalization gaps and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of examples selected by memorization influence, followed by retraining and comparison with equally sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because their measures address different claims. This does not dispute the reported theoretical directions. Neither the discussion of dropping rare examples nor the sample-cleaning discussion supplies V8's memorization-selected removal and random-removal comparison.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of natural labels with random labels, no held-out chance accuracy result, and no test of the listed architectures or recipes.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No sharpness or generalization-gap measure comparison.
No removal and retraining experiment on memorized examples.

rows.subject: model h
rows.size_stated: over-parameterized model, e.g. a deep neural network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of individual excessive generalization error when the model memorizes noisy labels for an instance.

conditions.value: noisy labels; memorization as defined in Definition 1

rows.measure: Individual excessive generalization error; lower bound scales with instance frequency and the empirical fraction of labels differing from the true label.
rows.value: Theorem 6 gives an Ω((l²/n²) · weight · sum of corrupted-label fractions) bound.
rows.note: The result is a theoretical bound for noisy-label memorization, not a measured natural-label test error.
rows.check: Theorem 6 is a conditional lower bound on individual excessive generalization error under noisy-label memorization, not evidence for any listed version. Retain its theoretical status and the assumptions inherited from Theorem 4.

rows.subject: neural network
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with synthesized noisy labels; examined loss distributions across training epochs.

conditions.value: instance-independent and instance-dependent synthesized label noise

rows.measure: Ability to separate clean instances from corrupted instances by loss distributions.
rows.value: The text states that in both noise cases, the neural network fails to separate clean instances from corrupted ones and memorizes a mixture of both.
rows.note: The text does not report numerical values for this result. Training setup details appear in Appendix B.
rows.check: The subject is ResNet-34, specified in Appendix B. Figure 3 plots normalized loss distributions, not held-out accuracy or a quantitative memorization rate. Overlap between clean and corrupted instances cannot establish V1.

rows.subject: h memorizing yLC
rows.operation_detail: Compared prediction error after memorizing the corrected label with error after memorizing the noisy label.

conditions.value: binary; non-trivial case with empirical noisy-label error greater than zero

rows.measure: Probability of predicting the wrong true label for the instance.
rows.value: With probability at least 1 − exp(−2l(1/2 − e_sgn(y)(x))²), memorizing yLC returns lower error.
rows.note: The result is conditional on the paper's assumption that the trained model can memorize yLC.
rows.check: This is a conditional theoretical comparison of loss correction with noisy-label memorization, assuming the model memorizes the corrected distribution. It does not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: h memorizing yLC
rows.operation_detail: Compared prediction error after memorizing the corrected label with error after memorizing the noisy label.

conditions.value: binary; non-trivial case with empirical noisy-label error less than one

rows.measure: Probability that loss correction produces higher prediction error than memorizing the noisy label.
rows.value: Theorem 8 gives a lower bound of 1/√(2l) · exp(−l·DKL(1/2 || e_sgn(y)(x))).
rows.note: This is a theoretical probability bound for noisy-label correction, not a natural-label generalization result.
rows.check: The higher-error probability concerns loss correction versus noisy-label memorization. It is not a reversal of any listed version; the result is a theoretical bound.

rows.subject: h memorizing yLS
rows.operation_detail: Compared prediction error after memorizing a smoothed label with error after memorizing the corrected label.

conditions.value: binary; E+ holds: empirical noisy-label frequency for +1 exceeds that for −1

rows.measure: Relative prediction error for the true label.
rows.value: Memorizing yLS leads to higher error than memorizing yLC.
rows.note: The paper states the opposite comparison when Ē+ holds; see R6.
rows.check: Add the explicitly stated condition that the true label is y = +1 and the empirical corrupted-label fraction lies in (0,1). Theorem 9 compares label smoothing with loss correction, not dropout or another listed version.

rows.subject: h memorizing yLS
rows.operation_detail: Compared prediction error after memorizing a smoothed label with error after memorizing the corrected label.

conditions.value: binary; Ē+ holds: empirical noisy-label frequency for +1 is less than that for −1

rows.measure: Relative prediction error for the true label.
rows.value: Memorizing yLS has lower error than memorizing yLC.
rows.note: This result is conditional on the empirical label-frequency event.
rows.check: Add the explicitly stated condition that the true label is y = +1 and the empirical corrupted-label fraction lies in (0,1). This conditional label-smoothing result does not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: h trained using peer loss
rows.stage_stated: trained using peer loss with cross-entropy loss
rows.operation_detail: Compared prediction error after peer-loss training with error from memorizing noisy labels.

conditions.value: class-dependent binary noise; n sufficiently large

rows.measure: Probability of predicting the true label and resulting individual excessive generalization error.
rows.value: With probability at least 1 − exp(−2l·p_sgn(−y)²·(1 − e+ − e−)²), peer loss predicts the true label; the paper says this improves individual excessive generalization error.
rows.note: The result is theoretical and conditional on class-dependent noise and the stated setup.
rows.check: Theorem 11 bounds the probability that confidently predicting the true label yields smaller peer training loss; it does not directly measure a trained network's probability of predicting correctly. Corollary 2 derives a generalization improvement within the theoretical setup. Neither tests a listed version.

rows.subject: h trained using peer loss
rows.stage_stated: trained using peer loss with cross-entropy loss
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed when peer loss favors predicting the wrong label over the true label.

conditions.value: binary; non-trivial case with empirical noisy-label error less than one

rows.measure: Probability that predicting the wrong label leads to smaller peer training loss, and corresponding prediction error.
rows.value: Theorem 12 gives a lower bound of 1/√(2l) · exp(−l·DKL(1/2 || e_sgn(y)); the text says this implies higher prediction error than memorizing noisy labels.
rows.note: The theorem concerns a theoretical probability of lower peer training loss for a wrong prediction.
rows.check: Theorem 12 concerns when confidently predicting the wrong label yields smaller peer training loss, under the class-dependent binary-noise setup continued from Theorem 11. Restore the complete exponent as -l·DKL(1/2 || e_sgn(y)). The extracted '1/1' is spurious. Higher error here is not a reversal of a listed version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
